items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: They’re great musicians, Ornette Coleman, the one they call the Doctor… Bowie?

ctx.x: Did you ever find yourself in a situation playing more avant garde styles or context? Were you ever at all attracted to that kind of music when it first hit the scene. For example, Ornette Coleman, the so-called free jazz….

Well, who am I to say what’s right and what’s wrong? I never could get with that music, so I would never reiterate on it because somebody likes it, ‘cause he works quite a bit and he makes quite a bit of money, so I just don’t know what they’re playing. It’s above me. So, I like the simpler things. They’re great musicians, Ornette Coleman, the one they call the Doctor… Bowie?

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: the same people that have been saying Ornette Coleman, John Coltrane, they go overboard for this.

ctx.x: So why, why, why do that? Why? You should be able to answer that more --

It's a form of white prejudice. There's no question about it. The only thing is, where I find it very hypocritical, here he comes along, now, if I said to one of these people now, I've been playing Ben Webster, Don Byas, Lester Young, Coleman Hawkins records, and I never play Coltrane's records because I can't stand them. Now they will say that I'm living in the past. But the same people, when this kid comes along, and he deserves a lot of credit because he's reviving something that deserves reviving, but the…
See, they don't listen. They can't be bothered to listen to Ben Webster on the old records, and so on.
